why: Tree DP with three states per node (has a camera, covered by a child, not yet covered), filled bottom-up: a node's state is forced by its children, which also yields the greedy 'put the camera on the parent of an uncovered leaf'.
hints: Leaves should never hold a camera: a camera on the leaf's parent covers strictly more. Start reasoning from the bottom.
Return one of three states from each subtree: 0 = this node is not covered yet, 1 = covered without a camera, 2 = has a camera. A null child counts as covered.
If any child is 0, place a camera here (return 2); else if any child is 2, return 1; else return 0. Add one more camera if the root ends at 0. O(n).
pitfalls: The root may be left uncovered at the end; it needs its own camera.
Treat missing children as covered, otherwise you put cameras on leaves.
statement:
You are given the root of a binary tree. You may install cameras on its nodes. A camera at a node monitors that node, its parent (if any) and its immediate children.

Return the minimum number of cameras needed so that every node of the tree is monitored.

Example: root = [0,0,null,0,0] (a root with one left child, which has two children). One camera on the left child monitors the root, itself and both of its children, so the answer is 1.

For a path of 5 nodes, cameras on the 2nd and 4th nodes cover everything, so the answer is 2.
constraints:
• The tree has between 1 and 1000 nodes.
  • Every node value is 0.
